article_title: A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement
citation: Emilyn Ruble Whitesell. (2016). A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, vol. 53, issue 7. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-day-at-the-museum-the-impact-of-field-trips-on-middle-school-science-achievement
title: Schools can provide enrichment experiences such as field trips without sacrificing student test scores
description: This principle holds that enrichment experiences like field trips are compatible with, rather than in tension with, academic accountability pressures. The study's evidence indicates field trips "can contribute positively to student achievement," so shifting resources toward them need not depress standardized test performance. It is grounded in a quasi-experimental analysis of New York City eighth-grade science exam outcomes.
requirements: Field trips must be to informal science education institutions for the studied effects to apply
constraints: Effects were estimated for middle school students in New York City on a standardized eighth-grade science exam
target_learning_goals: science achievement on standardized assessments
examples: The study found small positive effects of field trip exposure on science test scores and proficiency using school fixed effects across 6 years of student-level data
key_sources: Emilyn Ruble Whitesell. (2016). A Day at the Museum: The Impact of Field Trips on Middle School Science Achievement. Journal of Research in Science Teaching, vol. 53, issue 7. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-day-at-the-museum-the-impact-of-field-trips-on-middle-school-science-achievement

article_title: National Evaluation of Early Reading First
citation: Jackson, R., McCoy, A., Pistorino, C., Wilkinson, A., Burghardt, J., Clark, M., Ross, C., Schochet, P., Swank, P., & Schmidt, S. (2007). National Evaluation of Early Reading First: Final Report to Congress. Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Enhance preschool teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments to prepare children for school
description: The Early Reading First program embodies the principle that improving preschool quality on three fronts — teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments — helps children start school ready. Grants were "designed to enhance teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments in preschools to ensure that young children... start school with the skills needed for academic success."
requirements: Funding (grants) to preschools to support changes across teacher practices, instructional content, and classroom environments.
constraints: Evaluated in preschool settings serving young children, especially those from low-income families.
target_learners: preschool children, especially those from low-income families
target_learning_goals: school-entry language and literacy skills
examples: The federal program awarded grants to preschools, and the national evaluation found significant positive impacts on classroom and teacher outcomes and on children's print and letter knowledge.

article_title: Delivering on the Promise of Digital Equity
citation: Weaver, D'Andre J., Ph.D. (2022). Delivering on the Promise of Digital Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Close digital divides by engaging underrepresented communities in planning rather than paving over their interests, as interstate highway construction did
description: Drawing an analogy to the 1956 Interstate Highway Act, whose planners "physically paved over and uprooted established Black and poorer communities," the report argues today's digital infrastructure planners must instead plan with and learn from underrepresented communities and act on what is heard. It states that "the requirements of the new digital equity grant programs, the moral choice, and the pathway to finding the best solutions all lead to engaging and coordinating with these communities in new and significant ways," ensuring community ideas, interests, and needs manifest in state implementation strategies.
requirements: State planners must devote time, effort, and money to engagement and coordination with communities and the municipalities and nonprofits that serve them
constraints: The report cautions this engagement "is essential to success—not a grant obligation that simply needs to be met"
target_learners: students and families in historically and systematically excluded communities
target_learning_goals: equitable digital access, skills, and use for full participation in society and the economy
examples: Lindsay Unified's year-long community engagement effort with more than 200 parents in 2006-07 produced the district vision for 24/7 access to learning that anchored its digital equity transformation
key_sources: Weaver, D'Andre J., Ph.D. (2022). Delivering on the Promise of Digital Equity. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/38939984-18ea-4af0-8081-c787ac30d48d

article_title: Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas
citation: Pakhira, D., & Fusco, J. (2022, October). Designing for the future of research: Putting equity-relevant research into practice with scenarios and personas. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/163
title: Engage teachers, students, and families as partners in research throughout the development process, using participatory design research
description: The article's second recommendation is to include research participants, not only researchers, through participatory design research (PDR) and community-engaged research. Engagement should happen "throughout the development process and not just at the end," enabling platform developers to acknowledge students' cultural diversity and accommodate multiple modes of learning. The article notes this inclusion leads to buy-in and increases the relevance of the work, but requires time, resources, and compensation for community members.
requirements: Time and resources to support community participation, with acknowledgment and compensation for their work
Careful attention to the traditional roles of power in research, as PDR works to create new roles and relations
constraints: Working to include community members takes time and resources to support
target_learning_goals: improving equity in research
helping platforms interpret learners' preconceptions and experiences
examples: The article cites Hammond's point that cultural responsiveness informs practice so better teaching choices can be made for all students

citation: Russell, Christina A. (2023, April). Centering wellbeing: Advancing social emotional learning for all. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/177
title: Engage both decision makers and implementors in professional learning experiences to ease translation into district practice
description: The report's second readiness factor holds that districts translate working-group lessons into action more easily when leaders with authority for both decision-making and implementation participate together. In Suffern, the director noted the superintendent "heard [the ideas] directly," removing the need to plead the case; in El Segundo, clarity in roles let the superintendent secure board funding while the associate superintendent led program work.
requirements: Participation by leaders with authority for both decision-making and implementation
target_learning_goals: adopting and enacting SEL and wellbeing strategies district-wide
examples: Suffern's superintendent and counseling director attended together; El Segundo's superintendent and associate superintendent divided roles for funding and program design.

article_title: Scaling Career Pathways Statewide: A Blueprint for Creating K-12 + Postsecondary + Industry Pathways
citation: Scaling career pathways statewide: A blueprint for creating K-12 + postsecondary + industry pathways. (2026). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/287
title: Journey maps structured as entry, action, and goal for learners and school systems
description: The blueprint uses journey maps as a reusable design structure for codifying success criteria. It states: "The purpose of journey maps are to understand and codify the criteria for success by mapping the steps in the pathways journey," with each map structured as entry, action, and goal. Two scenarios are mapped: a learner journey for a high school student completing college and career readiness graduation requirements, and a school system journey for a system creating the conditions enabling that completion.
requirements: Mapping both the learner journey and the supporting school-system journey to align program supports and eliminate learner barriers
target_learners: high school students on college and career readiness pathways
target_learning_goals: completing college and career readiness graduation requirements
earning stackable credentials and CTE pathway completer status
examples: The learner journey map runs from learners aware of and enrolling in a high school pathway, through acquiring competencies and earning stackable credentials, to goals such as attaining high school CTE pathway completer status

article_title: Pre-Referral Processes in California State Preschool Programs: How Practitioners Decide to Refer Multilingual Children for Special Education Evaluation
citation: Burr, E., Burho, J., & Perez, A. (2023). Pre-Referral Processes in California State Preschool Programs: How Practitioners Decide to Refer Multilingual Children for Special Education Evaluation. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Ensure high-quality early learning, including home language support, before referring an ML child for special education evaluation
description: The report holds that before referring an ML child for special education evaluation, programs must ensure high-quality early learning so that lack of opportunity to learn can be ruled out as a contributing factor. This includes supports for the home language and partnering with families to promote continued home language use. Interviewees described supplementary language programs, at-home activities, and social-emotional approaches used to rule out behavior before referral.
requirements: Supports for the home language, including partnering with families to promote continued use of the home language
constraints: Additional educator training may be needed so limited language fluency is not mistaken for a special need
target_learners: Multilingual children in California State Preschool Programs
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing language need from disability-related need before special education referral
examples: One site ran a supplementary weekly language program in which family members participated alongside children and received at-home activities; teams used trauma-informed care, Conscious Discipline, and Pyramid Teaching to rule out behavior.

article_title: Access to Powerful Technology as a Catalyst for Career Pathway Engagement
citation: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217
title: Engagement funnel framework: awareness, interest, and engagement as stages of influence on occupational identity
description: The paper adapts Callahan et al.'s (2019) funnel of influences on occupational identity into a narrowed "engagement funnel" of awareness, interest, and engagement, used as the organizing coding scheme for interviews and observations. The authors state they "focused our attention on the earlier stages of influence to create an 'engagement funnel' of awareness, interest, and engagement, where awareness and interest are a more nuanced view on exposure." Movement along the funnel is described as not necessarily linear, with the stages interrelated.
requirements: Data on student and educator experiences must be coded against the funnel stages to trace transitions
constraints: The paper states deep levels of participation were not expected within the implementation timeline, so participation stages were excluded
target_learners: historically and systemically excluded (HSE) high school students
target_learning_goals: career and technical education (CTE) pathway awareness, interest, and engagement; occupational identity development
examples: The authors analyzed Anaheim High School interviews and observations using the engagement funnel coding scheme, then examined examples for powerful learning principles

article_title: Rural Turnaround: Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Rural Turnaround: Challenges and Opportunities. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://centeronschoolturnaround.org/journeys
title: Cultivate an environment of success and collaboration to attract teacher and leader recruits to rural turnaround schools
description: The article's recommended approach to rural recruitment goes beyond incentives: rural schools and districts should "create an environment where enthusiastic, committed, and effective teachers and leaders want to be." As the handbook states, "An environment of success and collaboration is attractive to potential recruits." Amargosa's principal recruits by telling candidates the work will be challenging but that the school has a multiyear, comprehensive plan for helping students learn and thrive.
requirements: A credible, multiyear, comprehensive improvement plan that can be honestly presented to potential hires
constraints: Recruitment remains difficult in remote communities regardless; Amargosa still lost more than half its teachers before implementation
target_learners: Teachers and school leaders considering employment in rural turnaround schools
target_learning_goals: Recruiting and retaining effective educators in hard-to-staff rural schools
examples: Principal Robert Williams tells potential hires the work will be challenging but that Amargosa has a multiyear, comprehensive plan for helping students learn and thrive

article_title: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity
citation: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity. (2021). Spencer Foundation & Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/summer-learning-creating-equity
title: Engage students' and families' knowledge and experiences in disciplinary learning rather than treating home lives as deficits
description: This principle holds that human learning is ecological and cultural, and that academic learning expands when it connects to learners' prior knowledge, experiences, and identities. The report warns that deficit views of students of color, low-income families, and multilingual learners drive remediation-oriented pedagogy, and urges that "children actively construct knowledge based on their experiences, relationships, and social contexts." Teachers build on this by inviting family and community expertise into disciplinary study, as in the Algebra Project's use of urban transit experiences for mathematics.
requirements: Educators must seek to understand learners' experiences and provide multiple opportunities to connect knowledge-building to personally relevant topics and lived experiences
constraints: The report notes learning environments all too often view students and families through a deficit lens, which must be actively countered
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly students of color, low-income families, and multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary learning in literacy, mathematics, and science connected to students' lived experiences
examples: In science classrooms studying plant growth, students measure plant height and soil moisture and interview family members who garden about how they keep plants healthy
key_sources: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity. (2021). Spencer Foundation & Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/summer-learning-creating-equity

article_title: Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: From Provision to Student Enactment
citation: Omar Alsaiari, Nilufar Baghaei, Jason M. Lodge, Naomi Winstone, Dragan Gašević, Hassan Khosravi. (2026). Making AI-Generated Feedback Matter: A Large-Scale Study of Feedback Workflows and Student Enactment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11625
title: Enacted Feedback workflow: staged selection, evaluative prioritisation, and selection-anchored AI dialogue
description: A reusable workflow pattern in which AI-generated feedback comments are the entry point to a staged process rather than a completed output. As the article states, "The workflow scaffolded three behaviours associated with productive feedback use that theDirected FeedbackandSelf-Directed Feedbackconditions left to students' discretion: student agency through selection, evaluative judgement through prioritisation, and dialogic engagement through targeted AI assistance." Students receive initial comments (A1), select improvement suggestions (A2), and enter AI dialogue anchored to those selections (A3), while retaining paths to bypass the structured pathway.
requirements: AI-generated feedback comments organised as strengths and suggestions for improvement
an interface that renders suggestions as selectable items and passes selections into the dialogue context
constraints: Students who bypass selection receive unanchored dialogue resembling the optional, student-initiated interaction of the Self-Directed condition
target_learners: higher education students authoring learning resources
target_learning_goals: feedback enactment
evaluative judgement
revision of drafted work
examples: In RiPPLE, 63.0% of Enacted Feedback resources moved from AI Feedback to selected suggestions, and the condition showed the highest uptake and revision counts

article_title: The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness
citation: Rose Niousha, Samantha Boatright Smith, Bita Akram, Peter Brusilovsky, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, John DeNero, and Narges Norouzi. (2026). The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05648
title: Engagement-based evaluation framework for AI tutors (RelScore and SuccScore)
description: The framework extends AI tutor evaluation with a behavioral dimension grounded in student interaction data, complementing pedagogical assessment. It quantifies "engagement qualityof tutor feedback by examiningwhetherandhowstudents used the AI tutor's feedback, conditioned on their subsequent code revisions". An LLM judge labels each feedback sentence for relevance (whether it influenced the student's code edit) and success (whether the suggested change was applied correctly), yielding RelScore, the fraction of feedback sentences students engage with, and SuccScore, the fraction of engaged feedback applied correctly.
requirements: A directional success criterion must be definable for the domain, e.g. subsequent code revisions in programming or next-response movement toward desired understanding in dialog-based tutoring
Logged consecutive submissions per student-problem pair so feedback can be compared against the following revision
LLM-judge annotation with human agreement validation
constraints: Metrics measure immediate feedback uptake, not longer-term learning outcomes

RelScore and SuccScore measure alignment between feedback and code edits rather than direct feedback reading, making revisions not driven by feedback hard to distinguish; large-scale rewrites or partially adopted suggestions complicate attribution
target_learning_goals: effective use of AI tutor feedback in programming problem solving
examples: Applied to 10,235 code submissions with AI tutor feedback from an introductory programming course, comparing two deployed tutors across Fall 2024 and Fall 2025
key_sources: Rose Niousha, Samantha Boatright Smith, Bita Akram, Peter Brusilovsky, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, John DeNero, and Narges Norouzi. (2026). The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05648

article_title: CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora
citation: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608
title: Implement engagement as an explicit typed contract rather than a global instruction to be more engaging
description: The article recommends that engagement moves in generated instruction be enforced as structured output fields rather than requested in prose. Without "a structured output schema, the model may produce fluent narration while omitting the instructional moves that sustain attention and connect concepts." Casting engagement as a typed contract also makes it measurable, since regex counts of analogies and retrieval prompts can be cross-checked against typed fields, and it makes ablations cleaner because a module is disabled by replacing its typed object.
requirements: Typed output schemas with closed enumerations and post-validators for each narration
Post-validation checks on required fields and word count, with regeneration on failure
constraints: Demonstrated in asynchronous generated lecture video grounded in a course corpus; the reported evidence covers only the engagement module ablation on five in-corpus topics with one persona
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention through hooks, retrieval prompts, analogies, and forward links in instructional narration
examples: The full pipeline's sinogram narration contained a hook, prior-concept callback, analogy, and forward link, while the ablated variant produced a roughly 31-word glossary fragment with none of these moves

citation: Dai, Z., Huang, F., Xiong, J., Yang, Y., Zhang, Q., & Peng, X. (2026). Inquiry-based learning in STEM education: the impact of generative AI-based Chatbots on primary school students’ problem posing ability in science. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00631-0
title: ENA network model of problem posing with eleven category and quality codes
description: This element is the article’s ENA modeling setup for analyzing students’ cognitive structures during problem posing. Because ENA focuses on associations among semantic units rather than frequency, "only 11 codes from question category (IQ, SC, SL, SR, OD, and CQ) and question quality (R, P , A, E, and C) were retained as network nodes". Lines between nodes represent co-occurrence relationships and line thickness indicates connection strength. Mean networks were constructed for phases and groups, with subtracted networks used to compare conditions, using the online tool epistemicnetwork.org.
requirements: Coded question data from the number-excluded category and quality coding scheme
Modeling conducted with the epistemicnetwork.org online tool
constraints: The quantity dimension was excluded as network nodes because ENA models associations among semantic units rather than frequency

examples: Subtracted networks compared cognitive structures between the experimental and control groups across pre-test, inquiry process, and post-test phases

article_title: EduGage: Methods and Dataset for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning
citation: Zikang Leng, Edan Eyal, Yingtian Shi, Jiaman He, Yaqi Liu, and Thomas Plötz. (2026). EduGage: A Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Ubiquitous Technol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01238
title: Deploy engagement sensing for broad temporal patterns and support triggers, not for exact point-level prediction of self-reported attention difficulty
description: Because engagement is partially latent and the self-report target is subjective, the article argues wearable sensing can only approximate moment-to-moment dynamics. The authors write that "in practical learning systems, such models may be most useful for identifying broader temporal patterns, such as sustained increases in attention difficulty or video segments where learners may benefit from reflection, review, or support" rather than expecting perfect agreement with self-report.
requirements: Models that capture meaningful temporal structure in attention difficulty, evaluated with participant-independent splits so performance reflects generalization to new learners
constraints: Exact self-reported scores remain difficult to predict; prediction discrepancies are expected because self-reports are subjective and physiological signals are indirect and may reflect fatigue, prior knowledge, video difficulty, movement, or distraction
target_learners: college students in self-guided asynchronous video learning
target_learning_goals: identifying periods of sustained attention difficulty and video segments needing review or support
examples: The authors report that a representative prediction trace captures coarse temporal trends even when exact point-level agreement with each self-reported rating remains difficult

article_title: From Heuristics to Analytics: Forecasting Effort and Progress in Online Learning
citation: Eric S. Qiu, Danielle R. Thomas, Boyuan Guo, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). From Heuristics to Analytics: Forecasting Effort and Progress in Online Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12788
title: Engagement forecasting as a supervised week-ahead prediction task in ITS
description: Engagement forecasting is framed as a supervised prediction task estimating a learner's next-week engagement from prior ITS interaction traces. The article defines it as "a supervised, week-ahead regression task within an ITS predicting two observable outcomes: minutes practiced (effort) and new skills mastered (progress)". It complements fine-grained EDM tasks (affect detection, wheel-spinning, dropout prediction) by operating at a weekly timescale aligned with instructional rhythms, and its explainability analysis positions forecasts as decision-support signals for tutors and students rather than direct measures of motivation or learning.
requirements: ITS log data with timestamps, durations, and skill mastery tags sufficient to construct weekly student-week targets and the four feature groups
constraints: Targets are explicitly simple, observable proxies, not complete measures of motivation or learning
Findings are restricted to a single ITS, subject domain, and platform-specific logging; the article does not claim the exact model or feature stack generalizes to other contexts
target_learning_goals: sustained weekly practice effort
week-to-week learning progress in mathematics skills
examples: Weekly targets built by aggregating ISO-week minutes and counting new AFM-mastered skills from 425 students over 39 weeks

citation: Yongkyung Oh, Lynn Talton, Alex Bui. (2026). Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction. KDD 2026 AI for Education Day, at the ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '26). https://kdd2026.kdd.org
title: Engagement intensity as a pair of complementary intake features (reported use and self-rated familiarity) for learner modeling
description: The article introduces engagement intensity as a working label for two complementary intake indicators of technology engagement drawn from technology acceptance and AI literacy research: "reported use and self-rated familiarity." It functions as a lightweight learner-modeling signal for intake-level grouping, explicitly scoped to pre-instruction segmentation rather than adaptive sequencing, personalized feedback, or a full intelligent tutoring system. In this framing, behavioral usage frequency is the primary axis and familiarity a secondary, self-perception-based check on perceived readiness.
requirements: Both features must be collected as short pre-instruction survey items before instruction begins
constraints: The article defines adaptive as intake-level learner grouping only, not differentiated materials, adaptive sequencing, personalized feedback, or a full intelligent tutoring system
target_learners: graduate and postdoctoral bioscience trainees in research ethics instruction
target_learning_goals: intake-level learner profiling for adaptive AI ethics instruction

article_title: Bridging Artificial Intelligence and Power Systems Education Using a Hands-On Executable Framework
citation: Junjie Yin, Buxin She, Xinyu Feng, Fangxing (Fran) Li. (2026). Bridging Artificial Intelligence and Power Systems Education Using a Hands-On Executable Framework. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02599
title: Engineering-Grounded AI (EGAI): AI workflows conforming to engineering and domain rules
description: EGAI is the design principle that "AI systems for power and energy applications should be developed so that every stage of their operation (input, routine, skills, workflow, iteration, verification, and output) conforms to established engineering principles and power-system domain rules, rather than treating the model as a task-agnostic black box." Each library module embodies this in miniature: inputs carry physical meaning, workflows are constrained by domain structure such as a power-flow solver or the swing equation, and outputs are verified against physical or analytical references before being trusted. The article positions EGAI as the principle learners should carry into their own work, countering passive reliance on LLMs.
requirements: Making engineering constraints visible and executable, with each output explicitly verified against a physical or analytical reference before it is trusted
target_learners: power and energy engineering students, researchers, and practitioners using AI
target_learning_goals: dependable, domain-constrained AI tool development rather than black-box or LLM-reliant use
examples: Module inputs are bus injections, states of charge, or system parameters; each output is verified against a power-flow solver result, an analytical solution, or a physical reference.

article_title: Illuminating complex student realities of artificial intelligence through an entangled pedagogy framework
citation: Fawns, T., Bearman, M., Corbin, T., Henderson, M., McLean, J., Matthews, K. E., Oberg, G., Liang, Y., & Walton, J. (2026). Illuminating complex student realities of artificial intelligence through an entangled pedagogy framework. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01730-1
title: Entangled pedagogy as a lens for analysing student engagement with generative AI
description: Entangled pedagogy (Fawns, 2022) positions technology as integral to educational activity, "foregrounding its inseparability with context, purpose, values, and educational methods." The article applies it to three students' GenAI accounts, finding that the framework's "five initial categories—technology, methods, purposes, values, and context—were entangled with other considerations, including beliefs, identities, emotions, positionalities, and the perceived actions of others." It treats pedagogy as an emergent, distributed phenomenon co-produced through relations between teaching and learning.
requirements: Researchers make explicit decisions about what to include, exclude and foreground to bound the analysis, using selected excerpts as a viewfinder
constraints: All representations of entangled phenomena are necessarily partial; the article does not propose expanding the framework to every possible element
target_learning_goals: understanding how students negotiate GenAI in relation to studies, identities and practices
examples: The study analysed three participants from different focus groups as situated configurations of intersecting relations, using Barad's notion of agential cuts to bound the analysis

article_title: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI
citation: Xiaotian Su, Laura Rimell, Jiazheng Li, Amal Rannen-Triki, Ulrich Paquet, Lisa Anne Hendricks, Rida Qadri, Daphne Ippolito and Piotr Mirowski. (2026). Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01518
title: Engage-to-Unlock: engagement-based access as a productive-friction mechanism for GenAI
description: Engage-to-Unlock is an interaction method in which generative capabilities become available only after users show task-relevant engagement. The article describes it as "a form of productive friction in which access to generative capabilities responds to each writer's engagement rather than elapsed time alone." In argumentative writing, the Tell-me text-generation mode unlocks when the essay contains a complete position and at least one distinct argumentative development linked to that position, detected by an LLM-based discourse classifier (micro-averaged F1 of 91.5%, macro-averaged F1 of 83.6%). Until unlock, users work with a pedagogical Teach-me assistant.
requirements: An LLM-based discourse classifier to detect the required engagement elements (position and argumentative development) in the user's draft
A restricted assistant mode (Teach-me) available before unlock and a generative mode (Tell-me) gated behind the criterion
constraints: In the study, 9 of 107 Engage-to-Unlock participants (8.4%) did not reach the contribution criterion and never unlocked Tell-me
The mechanism was implemented and tested for argumentative writing, where engagement is reflected in a position and supporting rationale
target_learners: Adult crowd workers (Prolific participants) completing argumentative writing tasks
target_learning_goals: Developing one's own position and argumentative rationale before receiving generative AI text generation
Accurate evaluation of AI-generated content for evidence and reasoning errors
examples: In the controlled experiment, Tell-me became available when both a complete position and a supporting claim were detected, each contributing 50% to a circular progress indicator, with partial formulations contributing 25%

article_title: Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction
citation: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309
title: Require the tool's engagement pattern to match pen-and-paper proof engagement, since even small automation can cause dramatic transfer failures
description: The article's central design lesson is that a classroom proof assistant must not only force engagement but make the engagement pattern similar enough to pen-and-paper. The authors report "non-obvious lessons about the extent to which even small amounts of seemingly tedium-saving automation can lead to dramatic transfer failures": automating evaluation stepping in the first deployment left students unable to transfer, while requiring students to write out each evaluation step substantially improved transfer. Designers should audit which automated steps replace reasoning students must practice for on-paper assessment.
requirements: The tool must force users to think through all the steps they would need to learn to think through in order to write a proof on paper (Criterion 5).
constraints: This must be balanced against Criterion 8 (Minimal Tedium): the assistant should not obligate proof steps that would be elided on paper or require didactically trivial long tasks.
target_learners: students learning to write proofs independently of the tool
target_learning_goals: transfer of proof skills to pen-and-paper exams
examples: Between deployments, double-clicking green-highlighted reducible sub-expressions was replaced by requiring students to highlight a sub-expression, type what it steps to, and press a check button validating the step.

article_title: Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning
citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Encoder-only transformer with classification head adapted for numerical physiological data classification
description: The authors adapt the original transformer architecture for classification of tabular physiological data: the decoder is removed and a classification head (linear transformation followed by softmax over grade categories A–F) is added to the encoder output. Each physiological feature is treated as an individual token in the input sequence, with embedding and positional encoding preserving temporal structure, and multi-head self-attention capturing dependencies among physiological features. The article states, "Specifically, only the encoder component of the transformer was retained, as our task requires generating a single output—predicted performance category—rather than producing a sequential output," and reports this is the first attempt to implement transformer architecture to model academic outcomes using physiological signals.
requirements: Input physiological data embedded as dense vectors with positional encoding added to maintain sequence order; a classification head with softmax converts encoder output into grade-category probabilities
constraints: Tuned configuration used 8 heads, 3 layers, dropout probability 0, d_model 256, 128 hidden-layer neurons, batch size 128, and sequence length 128
target_learning_goals: predicting exam grade categories from multivariate physiological stress signals
examples: The adapted transformer achieved a mean test accuracy of 0.9039 ± 0.0081 over 30 replicates

article_title: Make or Take: How Students Navigate Self-Created and Instructor-Provided Cheat Sheets
citation: Helen Weixu Chen, Victoria Sakhnini, and Lesley Istead. (2026). Make or Take: How Students Navigate Self-Created and Instructor-Provided Cheat Sheets. ACM Trans. Comput. Educ. https://doi.org/10.1145/3834566
title: Encourage students to create their own exam cheat sheets within fair and inclusive structural constraints
description: The article recommends that "instructors may consider encouraging students to create their own cheat sheets, rather than relying on instructor-provided versions," arguing that creation functions as a form of self-regulated learning requiring students to prioritize, organize, and synthesize information. Fairness and integrity concerns are addressed by structural constraints such as limiting sheets to a double-sided page, and policies must remain inclusive by allowing pedagogically equivalent alternatives. The article reports no statistically significant performance difference between formats, so the recommendation rests on engagement and preparation behaviour rather than measured achievement.
requirements: Structural constraints on sheet size (e.g., a double-sided page) to cap what can be included
Alternatives such as typed formats or oral accommodations for students with disabilities or differing learning needs
constraints: No statistically significant performance differences were observed between the two formats on either exam
Findings come from a single senior-level course; choices may look different in introductory, differently structured, or online courses
target_learning_goals: information prioritization and organization
self-regulated learning
exam preparation
examples: In the study, students could choose either format for both exams with a one-double-sided-page limit; most chose self-created sheets (70% midterm, 79.6% final) and self-created users spent significantly longer preparing for the midterm.

title: ENGAGE game-based learning environment for middle school computational thinking

Students program devices with a visual block-based language to solve computational challenges across three levels (Introductory, Digital World, Big Data). article_title: Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader
citation: deWinstanley, P. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2004). Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader. Memory & Cognition, 32(6), 945-955. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194854
title: Encoding-retrieval match accounts of the generation effect (procedural and transfer-appropriate multifactor accounts)
description: The article describes two accounts of when generation advantages occur, both centered on the relationship between encoding and retrieval. In the procedural account, "participants generating information at study, as opposed to reading it, are more likely to engage in procedures during study that can be reinstated during the retention test." In the transfer-appropriate multifactor account, generation effects occur when the generation task focuses processing on the type of information a later test is sensitive to. The authors use these accounts to interpret both prior findings and their own first-paragraph generation advantage.
requirements: A generation advantage requires a match between the information or procedures strengthened during generation and those demanded by the retention test
constraints: Both accounts predict the advantage disappears when encoding and retrieval processes are mismatched
target_learners: adult learners in laboratory memory experiments
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied verbal material
examples: The authors propose that participants used contextual information to generate and then recall items, and that noticing this use led them to attend to contextual information when reading later paragraphs

article_title: Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research
citation: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106
title: Pair a low-intrusion environmental analysis with knowledge elicitation when studying cognition in busy clinical settings
description: The article recommends sequencing a minimally intrusive environmental scan before more intrusive knowledge elicitation. "Including at least two data collection methods is unique to our health care-setting adapted CTA framework. We developed this progression to minimize intrusion into the clinical environment." The environmental analysis identifies actors, barriers, facilitators, and policies, and refines interview guides and sampling for the subsequent knowledge elicitation step.
requirements: A priori identification of data collection methods and materials during planning
Iterative refinement of knowledge elicitation materials based on environmental scan findings
constraints: Designed for busy clinical environments where intrusion must be minimized

examples: The pilot used structured observations of morning teaching rounds before beginning CDM interviews after 12 site observations

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Environmental Detectives handheld AR environmental consulting simulation
description: Environmental Detectives (ED) is a handheld AR simulation engaging high school and university students in an environmental consulting scenario in which they role play as environmental scientists investigating health concerns linked to toxins in the water supply. Working in teams of two or three with one Pocket PC, one walkie-talkie, a printed map and a notepad, players identify the contaminant, chart its path, and devise remediation plans, collecting simulated field data, interviewing virtual characters, and synthesizing findings into case reports. By design, "no one player can obtain all of the requisite information in the allotted time."

constraints: In ED there is no role differentiation among players, and since all players use the same software they can potentially access the same information at the same time

planning investigations balancing quantitative and qualitative data
collaboration
examples: Nearly a dozen classes ran through ED, including a suburban high school environmental science class and a private all-girls high school chemistry class

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Engeström's expansive learning: horizontal or sideways learning among peers without a conventional knowledge hierarchy, useful for conceptualising dealing with the atypical
description: The article draws on Engeström's (2001) activity-theoretical notion of expansive learning, articulated in the context of workplace learning. Engeström "draws attention to what he calls horizontal or sideways learning and development in which problem solving occurs essentially through interactions among peers without resort to a conventional knowledge hierarchy". The authors find this a potentially useful way of conceptualising their category of dealing with the atypical, where no set procedure exists and learning must address a problem or contradiction, often crossing workgroup boundaries.
requirements: The construct presupposes a focus on the social and organisational context rather than on individual learning, with contradictions or atypical events as sources of change.
constraints: The article presents expansive learning as a potentially useful conceptualisation for dealing with the atypical, not as a framework validated against the study data.
target_learning_goals: Dealing with atypical problems for which no set procedure or process exists
examples: The authors link dealing with the atypical to expansive learning because such problem solving can require crossing boundaries of workgroups and practices, which the well-bounded notion of communities of practice cannot adequately capture.

citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8
title: To improve children's sentence production in written composition in the upper elementary grades, instruction should attend to enhancing executive functions, particularly planning and inhibition
description: The article draws an instructional implication from its longitudinal findings: "in order to improve children's sentence production in written composition in the upper elementary grades, attention needs to be paid to enhancing children's EF, and particularly planning and inhibition skills." The authors add that such training may be crucial because enhancing syntactic complexity positively impacts overall compositional quality.

constraints: The recommendation rests on longitudinal correlational prediction, not on a manipulated intervention in this study
target_learners: typically developing children in upper elementary grades (fourth to sixth)
target_learning_goals: sentence production and syntactic complexity in written composition
examples: The study found fourth-grade planning and inhibition predicted improvement in narrative syntactic complexity by sixth grade

title: Encourage learners with ADHD to engage in creative tasks that match their preferences and abilities, and reward their creative work
description: The article concludes that people with ADHD may excel in specific creative tasks that match their preferences and abilities, and that "Encouraging them to engage in such tasks and rewarding their creative work may help both themselves, as well as the people around them, to benefit from the positive side of ADHD." This principle directs educators and designers to select creative activities fitting the learner's skills and to add goal-directed incentives such as competition or rewards, which the studies show raise idea originality in ADHD.

Samples consisted of high-functioning, mainly university-educated adults with ADHD, limiting generalizability
The mechanism underlying the competition effect (monetary reward vs. outperforming an opponent) remains unclear

real-world creative achievement
sustained task engagement during open-ended tasks

article_title: Parent Praise to 1- to 3-Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Gripshover Sarah J., Romero Carissa, Dweck Carol S., Goldin-Meadow Susan, Levine Susan C. (2013). Parent Praise to 1-3 Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later. Child development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12064
title: Entity and incremental motivational frameworks: coherent belief systems about trait malleability
description: The article defines motivational frameworks as children's entity or incremental theories "in combination with the beliefs, attributions, attitudes and behaviors that go along with those theories". An entity theory holds attributes are fixed and unchangeable, leading to performance goals, negative views of effort and mistakes, and helpless responses to setbacks; an incremental theory holds attributes are malleable, leading to learning goals, positive views of effort, and mastery-oriented responses. The study measured these frameworks in both intelligence and sociomoral domains via a 24-item composite questionnaire.
requirements: Assessed via questionnaires probing beliefs about trait stability, learning versus performance goals, attributions for success and failure, and strategy generation
constraints: Measured in children aged 7-8 years in the intelligence and sociomoral domains
target_learning_goals: beliefs about the malleability of intelligence and sociomoral goodness
challenge preference and attributions for success and failure
examples: The 24-item questionnaire included items such as "Imagine a kid who thinks that a person is a certain amount smart, and they stay pretty much the same. How much do you agree with this kid?"

citation: Perez-Felkner L, Nix S and Thomas K (2017) Gendered Pathways: How Mathematics Ability Beliefs Shape Secondary and Postsecondary Course and Degree Field Choices. Front. Psychol. 8:386. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00386
title: Enhance girls' beliefs about their mathematics ability under challenge, supported by social support from teachers, mentors, parents, and peers
description: The article recommends enhancing students' — especially girls' — beliefs about their mathematics ability when encountering challenging material, because these beliefs predict advanced science coursework and PEMC major selection at every stage. It states that "social support—from teachers, mentors, parents, peers—could be a valuable tool to scaﬀold students through challenges" and help girls counter lower beliefs about their mathematics ability. Recent interventions aiming to build resilience and malleable conceptions of intelligence are cited as promising approaches.
requirements: Feeling challenged is treated as a normal and necessary part of learning, so support should scaffold students through challenges rather than avoid difficulty
constraints: The recommendation rests on longitudinal observational associations, not on a test of the interventions themselves

target_learning_goals: persistence in mathematics and science coursework and pursuit of PEMC degree fields
examples: The article cites science camps like SciGirls, recruiting girls into upper level science courses and extracurricular activities, informal science learning experiences, and increasing visibility of women scientists

It foregrounds what youth identify as relevant, significant, and valuable as they leverage knowledge, practices, and interests to make change, and pairs with framing theory to explain how youth define environmental issues.

environmental decision-making in place

article_title: Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies
citation: Aleknavičiūtė, V., Lehtinen, E., & Södervik, I. (2023). Thirty years of conceptual change research in biology – A review and meta-analysis of intervention studies. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100556
title: Distinction between knowledge enrichment and knowledge restructuring as two outcome types in conceptual change research
description: The review adopts the field's core distinction between two types of conceptual change. Knowledge enrichment is learning in which "new knowledge is simply added to existing knowledge structures, enriching the knowledge base", whereas knowledge restructuring (also called revision) is "a more demanding process that requires fundamental changes and restructuring of one's existing knowledge structures", in which existing concepts may take on new meanings and misconceptions are revised. The distinction grounds the review's coding of outcome-measure quality and its finding that many studies capture only enrichment. Either multiple-choice or open-ended formats can capture either type; what matters is deliberate item design.
requirements: Assessing restructuring with multiple-choice items requires deliberately planned items systematically comparing correct scientific concepts with widely held misconceptions, complemented by open-ended questions
constraints: The data collection method alone does not determine which type of conceptual change is captured
target_learners: learners at all educational levels studied, from kindergarten to university
target_learning_goals: distinguishing genuine restructuring of scientific concepts from simple addition of facts
examples: The review coded each study's outcome measures as enrichment or restructuring, resolving coder disagreements through discussion until inter-rater reliability reached 100%.

article_title: Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review
citation: Juliette C. Désiron, Julien Venni, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2026). Mapping the Heterogeneity of Emotional Design Features in Multimedia Research: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10138-3
title: Endogenous versus exogenous anthropomorphism: the semantic function of anthropomorphic design
description: The review distinguishes anthropomorphic cues that are visually embedded in the represented entity itself (endogenous) from those conveyed through contextual or metaphorical human associations (exogenous). Endogenous features can fulfil a semantic function by conveying content-relevant information, e.g. "representing viruses with an angry appearance to signify their danger or virulence". Following Mayer (2011), the review states "such endogenous visual characteristics should be favoured over an exogenous use, where the anthropomorphic characteristics do not relate to the content's information". The distinction was operationalised in the review's coding of 15 materials (Table 6, Fig. 4).
requirements: Anthropomorphic elements should bear endogenous meaning relevant to the instructional content to serve a semantic function.
constraints: Anthropomorphic depictions may risk introducing misconceptions about underlying scientific concepts, creating a trade-off between affective engagement and conceptual accuracy.
target_learners: learners of science topics in multimedia instruction
target_learning_goals: content comprehension through semantically meaningful visual representations
examples: Bülbül and Kuzu (2021) represented a protostar as a baby on a fluffy cloud, conveying its early stage of formation surrounded by interstellar dust.

Success depends on many factors beyond endowment, including ambition, manner, and home conditions

article_title: The dynamics of student engagement in cooperative science learning: a multimodal approach
citation: Ido Davidesco, Yushuang Liu, Kim Chaloner, Emma Laurent, Gabriella A. Ali, Sarah C. Creider, Sean Hughes, Laura Noejovich, Henry Valk, Dana Bevilacqua, David Poeppel & Suzanne Dikker. description: The article characterizes engagement as "a dynamic, multidimensional, and multi-level phenomenon that unfolds during real-world classroom collaboration." Building on the three-component view (behavioral, cognitive, affective) and the ICAP framework, it argues that ICAP's engagement modes "are not discrete or stable categories but ﬂuid states that learners continuously move between during learning." article_title: Mnemonic-trained brain tuning to a regular odd-even pattern subserves digit memory in children
citation: Yafeng Pan, Ning Hao, Ning Liu, Yijie Zhao, Xiaojun Cheng, Yixuan Ku and Yi Hu. (2023). Mnemonic-trained brain tuning to a regular odd-even pattern subserves digit memory in children. npj Science of Learning 8:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00177-8
title: Encoding-pattern versus processing-efficiency hypotheses of mnemonic training, instantiated as four theoretical models of neural change
description: The article contrasts two accounts of why mnemonic training works: the processing-efficiency hypothesis holds that "the cognitive processing of to-be- memorized materials consumes less cognitive resource after training", while the encoding-pattern hypothesis proposes altered encoding patterns, inferred from mnemonists mapping digit pairs to images at even positions. These are instantiated as four models (A–D) predicting post- versus pre-training neural activity by digit position odd versus even. The results, conforming to Model B, support the encoding-pattern account.
requirements: EEG measurement of encoding-phase neural responses (ERP and oscillatory power) to digits presented sequentially at known positions, before and after training
constraints: The authors note their analyses were insufficient to completely exclude processing-efficiency, which may involve efficient neural networks not detected in ERP and oscillatory power analyses
target_learners: developing children (primary or middle school students, mean age ~13 years)
target_learning_goals: short-term digit memory via the digit-image mnemonic
examples: Model B predicted differential neural activity between odd and even digit positions at post-training but not pre-training; the observed P200 and theta odd-even effects matched this prediction

title: Use encouraging question asking as a simple, scalable pedagogical component to foster valuation of new science information in young learners
description: The article recommends encouraging children to ask questions during science lessons, with teachers modeling question asking and praising children's questions, as an "efficient, scalable teaching method to bolster curiosity". Curiosity-driven question asking
Science learning
examples: Over eight one-on-one virtual lessons, children in the question-asking condition were told the purpose was to get really good at asking questions, teachers modeled questions, and questions were praised and answered

citation: Neil Selwyn. (2023). Constructive Criticism? Working with (Rather than Against) the AIED Back-Lash. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00344-3
title: Engage AIED criticism constructively rather than defensively
description: The article argues proponents should resist instinctive responses to fix, dismiss, or rebut critics, and instead "engage with what these criticisms are telling us about AIED". This means treating critics as raising points "worth unpacking in further detail", examining the specific applications, motivations and values behind the backlash rather than presuming critics lack technical understanding or educational vision.

Reflection on one's own positionality and the values driving one's work
constraints: The article explicitly recommends against proposing quick solutions or chiding critics for negativity

examples: RETAIN is proposed as the evaluation model for how endogenously content is embedded in a game's fantasy and story context

article_title: Understanding student engagement in online learning environments: the role of reflexivity
citation: Peter Kahn, Lucy Everington, Kathleen Kelm, Iain Reid, Francine Watkins. (2017). Understanding student engagement in online learning environments: the role of reflexivity. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9484-z

description: This framework theorises student engagement as the exercise of intentional human action, or agency, drawing on Archer's staged model in which agents configure concerns in structural settings and translate them into projects and practices. Reflexivity is the internal deliberation underpinning this: "the ordinary mental capacity to consider oneself in relation to one's social setting". The study applies the framework to online postgraduate environments, extending it with collective reflexivity, and finds it helps explain engagement while revising the single-dominant-mode claim.

constraints: The study examined engaged postgraduate students in fully online Masters programmes, and the methodology tended to select engaged rather than disengaged participants
target_learners: postgraduate students in fully online higher education
target_learning_goals: student engagement in online learning
examples: Interviews probed reflexivity with questions such as whether students paused to think about tasks, and discussion postings were coded for concerns and actions

article_title: Estimating Impacts of Treatment Random Assignment on Classroom Quality in the Head Start Impact Study: The Problem of Missing Data
citation: Friedman-Krauss, A. H., Connors, M. C., & Morris, P. A. (2013). Estimating impacts of treatment random assignment on classroom quality in the Head Start Impact Study: The problem of missing data. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2013s/
title: Endogenous missingness framework for estimating treatment impacts on classroom quality
description: The article frames missing classroom-quality data as a threat that is endogenous to treatment assignment rather than random: because a quality rating can only be collected when a child is in formal care, and Head Start increases formal care enrollment, "missingness" due to being in parental care is associated with randomization. The framework distinguishes three sources of missingness (parental care, unobserved formal settings, unknown care type) and models each as an outcome before estimating quality impacts.
requirements: Missingness must be modeled and accounted for before estimating unbiased intent-to-treat impacts on quality, as the article states unbiased impacts cannot be estimated without accounting for the association between missingness and random assignment.
constraints: Developed for the Head Start Impact Study context, where quality data were collected only in children's primary care settings and centers had knowledge of the study.
target_learners: 3- and 4-year-old low-income children in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: Improving the quality of children's early learning environments and school readiness skills
examples: The authors estimated impacts of random assignment on each of the three types of missing data using fixed effects for center groups, separately for 3- and 4-year-olds and the full sample.
key_sources: Friedman-Krauss, A. H., Connors, M. C., & Morris, P. A. (2013). Estimating impacts of treatment random assignment on classroom quality in the Head Start Impact Study: The problem of missing data. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org/conferences/2013s/

article_title: Reporting Randomized Controlled Trials in Education
citation: Evan Mayo-Wilson, Sean Grant, Paul Montgomery. (2014). Reporting Randomized Controlled Trials in Education. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Endorse reporting guidelines for education RCTs by journals, funders, and professional organizations to raise reporting quality
description: The article recommends that the CONSORT-SPI guideline be endorsed by journals, research funders, and professional organizations, because "Endorsement of the guideline by journals, research funders, and professional organizations will facilitate use of and feedback on the guideline". Dissemination is planned through simultaneous publication and endorsement in multiple journals, funder endorsement, conference presentations, and a dedicated website for feedback, which the authors expect will help raise reporting standards. This addresses the finding that most leading education journals do not ask authors to follow reporting standards.
requirements: Simultaneous publication and endorsement of the guideline in multiple journals, endorsement by funding agencies, and a dedicated website facilitating feedback
constraints: The guideline addresses reporting of intervention RCTs in education and related disciplines, not other study designs
target_learners: authors of education intervention RCT reports
target_learning_goals: improving the accuracy, comprehensiveness, and transparency of RCT reports in education
examples: The project's phase 5 plans dissemination with simultaneous publication and endorsement of the guideline in multiple journals, endorsement by funding agencies, presentations at conferences and other meetings, and a dedicated website that will facilitate feedback about the guideline
key_sources: Evan Mayo-Wilson, Sean Grant, Paul Montgomery. (2014). Reporting Randomized Controlled Trials in Education. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562867

article_title: SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Victoria Menzies, Clare Collyer, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2015). SHINE in Secondaries: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Engagement with School and Learning survey
description: An online pupil survey developed by the research team from a review of the engagement literature to measure engagement with school and learning as a secondary outcome. It covers identity with school (16 items), motivations at school (13 items), beliefs about ability (6 items), active participation in learning (15 items) and behaviour in completing school work (7 items), mostly on four-point Likert scales with all items positively worded. Initial analysis indicated reliability was best for the whole scale, so the total score was used as the outcome measure.
requirements: Scale validation and reliability evidence was still being gathered from this project and another pilot
constraints: The survey was still in its piloting phase at the time of use
target_learning_goals: engagement with school and learning
examples: Items include ‘I feel like part of the school’ and ‘I get involved in class discussions’

article_title: Enhancing Direct Instruction on Introductory Physics for Supporting Students' Mental-Modeling Ability
citation: Mansyur, J., & Darsikin. (2016). Enhancing Direct Instruction on Introductory Physics for Supporting Students' Mental-Modeling Ability. International Education Studies, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n6p32
title: Enhanced Direct Instruction (EDI) stages for introductory physics integrating DI patterns with macro- and micro-strategy
description: EDI is a lesson-level instructional pattern for introductory physics that maps Rosenshine's DI pattern onto stages such as eliciting initial knowledge, informing learning goals, gradually presenting material with exercises, lecturer modeling of problem-solving by thinking-aloud, emphasis on diagrams, guided initial practice, and systematic feedback. The article states that "Table 4 shows the integration of the principles of macro-strategy into DI pattern with micro-strategy forming EDI structure that is more specific but more complex." The final model drops the group reciprocal-teaching stage after formative reflection.
requirements: Operated through preparation of lesson plans as part of the development stage
Explicit instruction emphasizing the importance of the diagram and its simultaneous use with identification of given and required variables
constraints: The group reciprocal-teaching stage with student thinking-aloud was excluded after the lecturer had difficulty managing the class
target_learners: High school students to second-year university students in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: Mental-modeling ability, especially transforming external representations and manipulating mental models based on propositions
Concept mastery of Kinematics, Dynamics, and Work-Energy
examples: In the quasi-experiment, the experimental class followed the EDI stages over six lessons while the control class followed the DI model
key_sources: Mansyur, J., & Darsikin. (2016). Enhancing Direct Instruction on Introductory Physics for Supporting Students' Mental-Modeling Ability. International Education Studies, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n6p32

article_title: Investigating the Effect of Reduced Forms Instruction on EFL Learners' Listening and Speaking Abilities
citation: Mohammad Saber Khaghaninezhad & Ghasem Jafarzadeh. (2014). Investigating the Effect of Reduced Forms Instruction on EFL Learners' Listening and Speaking Abilities. English Language Teaching, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n1p159
title: Taxonomy of English reduced forms in connected speech
description: Drawing on Brown and Kondo-Brown (2006), the article organizes the phonological simplifications of informal native-speaker speech into named types: reduced forms such as /gonna/ and /wanna/, contraction (I'm, don't), elision (omission of /t/ in "last night"), reduction of unstressed vowels to schwa, and assimilation ("Don't you": /dontʃa/). The article states these involve "unstressed vowels, omitted sounds, and other alternation of the full form" and occur "in all levels of speech from casual to even very formal levels", making them a key obstacle for learners accustomed to carefully articulated classroom speech.
requirements: Learners need explicit attention to the sound changes and phonological rules of each type for the taxonomy to support instruction
constraints: The taxonomy concerns English connected speech; the article notes terminology varies across researchers (sandhi forms, weak forms, connected speech)
target_learners: EFL learners listening to authentic native-speaker speech
target_learning_goals: decoding connected speech
recognizing reduced forms
producing natural-sounding speech
examples: The experimental lessons taught the phonological rules of each type and had learners fill in blanks with complete forms of reduced forms they heard in taped statements
key_sources: Mohammad Saber Khaghaninezhad & Ghasem Jafarzadeh. (2014). Investigating the Effect of Reduced Forms Instruction on EFL Learners' Listening and Speaking Abilities. English Language Teaching, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n1p159

article_title: Effect of PowerPoint Presentation on Students' Cognitive Achievement in Geography
citation: Adams Ogirima Onivehu, Onyiyeche Emilia Ohawuiro. (2018). Effect of PowerPoint Presentation on Students' Cognitive Achievement in Geography. Romanian Review of Geographical Education, VII(1), 46-60. https://doi.org/10.23741/RRGE120184
title: Enrich Geography lessons with visual and auditory presentation features rather than teacher talk alone
description: The article argues instruction should appeal to multiple sensory modalities: PowerPoint slides with photographs, diagrams, animations and colour encode information into auditory and visual working memory for integration with prior knowledge, whereas chalkboard lecture is "majorly based on the teachers' talk". In the study, the experimental group received this enriched form while the control group heard verbal presentation only, and the enriched group achieved significantly more.
requirements: Presentation software with capacity for photographs, diagrams, animation, sound and colour
Hardware for display (laptop and LCD projector)
constraints: In the study, students did not access the slides before or after the lesson, so the principle was tested for in-lesson use only
target_learning_goals: Understanding of abstract Geography concepts such as soil erosion, rocks, and settlement functions
examples: Experimental-group lessons displayed animated slides with relevant photographs and diagrams while the teacher explained each slide and students listened, watched, and took notes
key_sources: Adams Ogirima Onivehu, Onyiyeche Emilia Ohawuiro. (2018). Effect of PowerPoint Presentation on Students' Cognitive Achievement in Geography. Romanian Review of Geographical Education, VII(1), 46-60. https://doi.org/10.23741/RRGE120184

article_title: The Relation between Teacher Vocabulary Use in Play and Child Vocabulary Outcomes
citation: Ragan H. McLeod, Ann P. Kaiser, and Jessica K. Hardy. (2019). The Relation Between Teacher Vocabulary Use in Play and Child Vocabulary Outcomes. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121418812675
title: Enhanced Milieu Teaching (EMT) as a naturalistic, play-based language intervention framework
description: EMT is described as "a well-researched, semistructured, play-based individualized intervention" implemented by teachers, parents, and clinicians, embedded in everyday activities and routines including play. It teaches functional language skills including vocabulary, early semantic relations, and syntax, using strategies such as language modeling in response to child communication and prompting language production in play. In this study, EMT sessions provided the interactional context in which teacher vocabulary use and supports were examined with children with low language skills in Head Start classrooms.
requirements: Teachers require training (approximately 15 hr in this study) and ongoing coaching to implement EMT strategies
constraints: Specific vocabulary supports such as gestural and oral supports and defining words in context are not defined specifically in the EMT model itself, per the article
target_learners: preschool children with low language skills in Head Start classrooms
young children at risk for language delays due to economic disadvantage
target_learning_goals: expressive vocabulary use
functional language skills including early semantic relations and syntax
examples: Teachers conducted two to three individual EMT sessions per week with thematic toy sets, a vocabulary probe, and a short story book, for approximately 60 sessions per child
key_sources: Ragan H. McLeod, Ann P. Kaiser, and Jessica K. Hardy. (2019). The Relation Between Teacher Vocabulary Use in Play and Child Vocabulary Outcomes. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0271121418812675

citation: Bada Tayo Abass. (2011). Computer Instructional Approach and Students' Creative Ability in Sculpture Education in Nigeria Universities: Obafemi Awolowo University as a Case Study. World Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v1n2p130
title: Encourage the use of computer graphics in teaching and learning sculpture education in Nigerian universities
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that computer graphics be used in sculpture education because, in its words, application of computers in learning environments influenced student performance. It states: "The use of computer – graphic in teaching and learning of sculpture education in Nigeria Universities should be encouraged." The recommendation rests on the study's ANCOVA and Scheffe results rather than on a demonstrated advantage over conventional teaching.
requirements: Availability of computer facilities in the learning environment, which the article notes many Nigerian schools lack
constraints: The supporting study was a single non-randomized pretest-posttest control group study at one university with 48 students
target_learning_goals: creative ability in sculpture skill development
examples: The study compared a computer-graphics-aided group with an expository method group of sculpture students using a researcher-developed Creative Ability test

description: A recurring activity program in which preschool sessions are enhanced with time-concept content and reinforced with concrete materials such as illustrated cards. The article reports that "activities that were enhanced with time concept and reinforced with materials prepared by the researchers were organized to be applied one hour a week for 10 weeks". Activities were planned from the Ministry of National Education Preschool Education Curriculum so children could express themselves easily, work in groups and individually, and perceive the time concept effortlessly.
requirements: Activities built on the Ministry of National Education Preschool Education Curriculum acquisitions and indicators appropriate to children's development
Concrete materials prepared in advance
Children's interests and needs considered in planning
constraints: Applied to children with normal development attending preschool institutions
target_learners: preschool children aged 60 months and older
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the time concept and its subconcepts
examples: Applied to the experimental group between 3rd of April 2017 and 10th of June 2017 while control children continued the standard curriculum
